source.title: What Causes Polysemanticity? An Alternative Origin Story of Mixed Selectivity from Incidental Causes
source.authors: Victor Lecomte; Kushal Thaman; Rylan Schaeffer; Naomi Bashkansky; Trevor Chow; Sanmi Koyejo

record.file_problem: The full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper presents theoretical and experimental evidence that polysemanticity can arise incidentally in toy autoencoders even when there are at least as many neurons as features, refining the capacity-based account.
record.gate_note: The paper's own results relevant to the versions are its analysis and experiments on incidental polysemanticity. It also reports changes in sparsity alone in Figures 2, 4, and 5; those do not themselves measure polysemanticity, so they are not rows. Cited results from other work are not recorded.
record.test_reason: Using theory and toy-autoencoder experiments, the paper argues that polysemantic neurons arise without capacity pressure (m ≥ n), through random initialization plus sparsity pressure from ℓ1 or bipolar noise. This bears directly on V3 and qualifies V2. It is not an original source.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is accurate. The authors present incidental polysemanticity as a second, non-mutually exclusive origin to the capacity story. It arises from random initialization amplified by sparsity-inducing training (ℓ1 or negative-kurtosis noise). They call for work on the performance–polysemanticity tradeoff and on distinguishing incidental from necessary polysemanticity.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a tied-weight shallow nonlinear autoencoder with basis-vector data and ℓ1 regularization or hidden-layer noise, focusing on incidental polysemanticity when m ≥ n rather than testing the original superposition regime.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported outcomes vary with hidden-layer size in the ℓ1 experiments and with noise type and magnitude in the sparsity experiments; Figure 6 examines one instance at σ = 0.01.
record.problems: The evidence is from toy autoencoders rather than LLMs. The paper reports 16 training runs for the Figure 3 trend but gives no uncertainty estimate or exact per-size values in the text. The Figure 6 example is one specific instance.
record.rows_left_out: Figures 2, 4, and 5 report sparsity measures such as fourth norms, but not polysemanticity itself. No results were omitted from the relevant polysemanticity findings.

untested.parts: Whether important features get dedicated dimensions while less important ones share; no regime with n > m and no variation in feature importance.
How prevalent incidental polysemanticity is in real or large networks (the authors pose this as an open question).
Entire version: no regime with more features than dimensions and no geometry analysis.
Entire version: no LLMs or SAEs.

missing.what: The introduction states that experiments confirm the polysemantic-neuron count is an asymptotic match for both models, but no count of polysemantic neurons is reported for the noise model.
A Section 5 statement, derived from r1's analysis, that incidental polysemanticity persists until the number of hidden neurons is roughly the number of features squared.

record.verdict_notes: All evidence comes from toy autoencoders with orthogonal basis-vector features. Figures 2, 4, 5 and 7 report sparsity (ℓ1 or fourth norms), not polysemanticity, and are correctly excluded as rows. No uncertainty estimates are reported. Normal noise produced no sparsification; this is relevant context, since only negative-excess-kurtosis noise drives the effect.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test the stated regime with more sparse features than dimensions, nor whether features form nearly orthogonal overlapping directions with regular geometry.
Does not test whether important features receive dedicated dimensions or compare feature importance. Tests whether polysemanticity can occur without a feature-to-neuron capacity shortage.
Tests incidental causes in toy autoencoders, not their prevalence in LLMs or other real-world networks.
No LLM activation or SAE evidence is tested.
Does not test whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical units.
Does not compare one-dimensional feature directions with multidimensional features.

rows.subject: non-linear autoencoder
rows.operation_detail: Analytically estimates benign collisions from random initial feature encodings.
rows.measure: Expected number of polysemantic neurons from benign collisions
rows.value: roughly n²/(4m); the text also gives Θ(n²/m)
rows.note: The analysis attributes these collisions to features initially having their largest coordinates in the same neuron with opposite signs; the stated setting has enough neurons to represent each feature separately.
rows.check: This is an analytic prediction (expected count ≈ n²/(4m) from benign collisions), not a measurement on a trained model. stage_stated 'trained' and operation 'measurement' should read theoretical derivation. Keep it as theory corroborated by r2.

source_check.correct: Theoretical estimate for the ℓ1-regularized tied-weight autoencoder with m ≥ n: expected benign-collision count n(n−1)/(4m), approximately n²/(4m). Operation should be theoretical derivation; the estimate is not a measurement on a trained checkpoint or restricted to the experimental width sweep.
source_check.locator_found: Sections 1.1, 2.1 and 2.5, especially the benign-collision calculation preceding the Figure 3 experiment.
source_check.problem: The subject's trained-stage annotation and measurement operation misclassify an analytic prediction.

rows.subject: non-linear autoencoder
rows.operation_detail: Trains the autoencoder with ℓ1 regularization and measures polysemantic neurons across runs.
rows.value: The reported trend is Θ(n²/m), and the constant 1/4 is described as fairly accurate.
rows.note: The text reports the trend across 16 runs but does not provide exact values for each hidden-layer size.
rows.check: Figure 3 states n = 256 (the text says n ≈ 256). Per-size counts are read only from the figure, so the value is qualitative: the Θ(n²/m) trend with a constant near 1/4 across 16 runs.

source_check.locator_found: Section 2.5, final experimental paragraph; Figure 3 caption.

rows.subject: non-linear autoencoder
rows.operation_detail: Trains the autoencoder with bipolar hidden-layer noise and inspects the learned encoding matrix.
rows.measure: Polysemantic encoding and its fourth norm
rows.value: Encoding W2 has significant weights in 7 coordinates chosen by other encodings; its fourth norm remains below 0.2.
rows.note: The authors explain the incomplete sparsification as an interplay between the push for sparsity and interference.
rows.check: This is a single illustrative instance (bipolar noise, σ = 0.01) and the size is not stated. The encoding W2 spreads across 7 neurons owned by other features, a different polysemantic configuration from r1/r2. No count or rate is given.

source_check.locator_found: Section 4, Figure 6 caption and accompanying paragraph: bipolar noise σ = 0.01; W2 shares 7 coordinates; ∥W2∥₄⁴ remains below 0.2.

relationships.condition: Tied-weight ReLU toy autoencoder, ℓ1 regularization, basis-vector data, m from 256 to 4096 ≥ n = 256
relationships.reason: Polysemantic neurons appear at the predicted Θ(n²/m) rate despite enough neurons for a monosemantic solution (r1, r2).
relationships.display_finding: Polysemantic neurons appeared at the predicted Θ(n²/m) rate even though the network had enough neurons for a monosemantic solution.
